caseno: Criminal Petition for leave to appeal No. 554 of 2010
lawyer:
Mrs. Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner 
Respondents ----- Not represented
parties:
Md. Kamal Uddin alias Md. Kamal Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Mezbah Uddin and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J.:- This criminal petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 18.07.2010 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 16195 of 2007 discharging the Rule. 

 2. The relevant facts, for disposal of the case, are that respondent No. 1 as complainant filed C.R. Case No. 77 of 2006 against the petitioner before the court of learned Magistrate, 1st Class, Kalapara, Patuakhali under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (the Act) alleging inter alia that the accused petitioner is the respondent's relative and he received Taka 6,50,000/- (six lac fifty thousand) from the respondent on different dates in cash and by cheque as loan for commercial purpose under the condition to return the loan money within two months. After the expiry of the stipulated time to return the money, the respondent went to the petitioner's office namely Nahar Biponi, Sadar Road, Barisal on 05.10.2005 and asked him to return the said money and the petitioner drew a cheque being No. CD-ID/CA 2831506 for Taka 6,50,000/- against the current account No. 001058707 of Janata Bank, Corporate Branch, Barisal. 

 3. After receiving the cheque, the respondent deposited it into his account No. SB 5578 of Janata Bank, Kalapara Branch, Patuakhali on 18.10.2005 and the authority of the bank sent the cheque to their relevant branch and thereafter on 24.10.2005 Janata Bank, Barisal Branch informed their Kalapara Branch about the insufficiency of fund to honour the cheque. On 06.11.2005 Janata Bank, Kalapara Branch returned the said cheque to the respondent giving a certificate of insufficiency of fund. Thereafter, on 08.11.2005 the respondent sent a legal notice to the petitioner through his lawyer which was received by the petitioner on 15.11.2005. The petitioner gave a reply to the said legal notice on 20.11.2005 which was received by the respondent on 23.11.2005. Thereafter, the respondent filed the aforesaid case against the petitioner. 

 5. Thereafter, the petitioner voluntarily surrendered before the court below and obtained bail. Subsequently, the case record was transmitted to the Court of Sessions Judge, Patuakhali for trial and the learned Sessions Judge took cognizance of the offence under the said section. 

 6. Thereafter, the case was transmitted to the Court of Assistant Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Patuakhali and the learned Judge of the said Court framed charge against the petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 rejecting an application under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure preferred by the accused petitioner. 

 9. Mrs. Sufia Khatun, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that since the complaint was instituted on 14.12.2005 before the promulgation of the Negotiable Instrument (Amendment) Act, 2006 the case is tribal by the Metropolitan Magistrate and as such framing of charge and holding of trial by the Sessions Judge is without jurisdiction. She further submitted that the amendment came into effect on 09.2.2006 which provides that no court inferior to the Court of Sessions, shall try an offence punishable under section 138 of the said Act and, therefore, an Assistant judge has no power to continue the trial of such a case and as such the proceeding pending before the learned 3rd Assistant Sessions Judge, Potuakhali, is an abuse of the process of the court. She submitted that therefore the High Court Division erred in law in not quashing the case. 

 11. It appears from the records that although the complaint was lodged before the amendment to the Act, which came into effect on 09.2.2006, the Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance of the case on 25.5.2006 after the amendment was brought into effect. The Magistrate, therefore, rightly transferred the case to the Court of Sessions which has the power to try the case under section 141 (c) of the Act, Hence, the submission of the learned Advocate-on-Record that the case must be tried by the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate is misconceived. 

 12. With regard to the submission that the Assistant Sessions Judge does not have jurisdiction to hear the matter, we may refer to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (the Code) which provides in section 6 that, apart from the Supreme Court and Courts constituted under any other law, there shall be two classes of criminal courts, namely Courts of Sessions and Courts of Magistrate. An Assistant Sessions Judge or Joint Sessions Judge as mentioned in section 9 (3A) of the Code is also a Judge of the Court of Sessions. Section 141 (c) provides that no court inferior to that of Court of Sessions shall try any offence punishable under section 138. The section does not say that any case under section 138 may not be tried other than by the Sessions Judge. The Court of Assistant Sessions Judge is also a Court of Sessions and as such there is no illegality in the trial continuing before the Court of Assistant Sessions Judge. Moreover, we may refer to a decision of this Division in the case of M.K. Bazlur Rahman Vs. Md. Johurul Haque and another reported in VI ADC (2009), 809, where this Division affirmed the judgment of the High Court Division which had held that: 

 "A criminal proceeding shall not be stifled before trial, when there was a prima facie case for going to the trial." 

 13. In that case also the charge had been framed under section 138 of the Act. In the instant case, the charge having been framed by a competent court, there is no justification in quashing the case at this stage. 

 14. The High Court Division has elaborately discussed the points in issue and decided that the proceeding of Session Case No. 12 of 2007 arising out of C.R. Case No. 77 of 2006 (Kalapara) under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not illegal.
